attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'will' forecast. 'Even after the bubble falls apart' is a fair reading of the context: the sentence follows his remark about collapse. No horizon is stated.

contract.note: Reading the claim as LLM technology surviving the collapse, not every company surviving, is fair and ordinary. Requiring an established collapse first matches the context. The contract correctly sets no deadline.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own disclosure of an October 2026 model release, dated before the evaluation date. It shows LLM development continuing, but no preceding broad collapse is established, so it cannot meet the support condition.

reviews.rationale: This is a forecast with no deadline. The early-resolution rule needs an established broad collapse followed by continued LLM availability. The packet establishes no collapse, so there is no conclusive event, and current existence alone cannot settle the claim. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A general causal claim that unreliability constrains profits. In context, 'AI' means LLMs. No threshold or scope is given.

contract.note: The plain reading (unreliability materially constrains LLM-business profits, without meaning zero profits) is ordinary and fair. The contract rightly separates customer losses from supplier profits.

evidence.note: ABC report of Deloitte's partial refund over an AI-assisted report with errors. This is one customer-side incident. It illustrates a possible mechanism but does not measure LLM-supplier profits or net effects.

reviews.rationale: The only item is a single customer-side refund anecdote. Nothing in the packet links reliability failures to measured LLM-supplier profits, and no counterevidence is offered. The general causal claim is not settled by the available evidence.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The claim has two parts: roughly USD 1 trillion has been invested, and the core technical problems are not remedied. The 'or so' approximation is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'remedied' as fixed enough for dependable performance, not as 'no improvement', is fair. Realized cumulative spending is an ordinary reading. The unspecified accounting basis is properly flagged.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own December 2025 disclosure. It concedes the model is still imperfect while reporting fewer errors. This bears on the remediation half only and does not set a representative reliability threshold. It says nothing about the investment total.
Stanford HAI figure for US private AI investment in 2024 alone. It is a different metric, period, and scope, so it cannot confirm or refute a cumulative total of about USD 1 trillion.

reviews.rationale: The monetary half is not established: no matched cumulative total of about USD 1 trillion is in the packet. The remediation half has only partial support, from a company disclosure admitting continuing errors. Because the claim joins both parts, the packet does not settle it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The causal claim and the 'in large part' qualifier are kept. The proposition also contains 'never will', but the contract leaves that to a separate forecast record. This record scores only the causal part.

contract.note: Requiring evidence that technical limits substantially cause the poor economics is a fair reading of 'in large part'. The ambiguity over supplier profits, customer returns, or valuations is flagged.

evidence.note: METR trial finding a productivity penalty in one early-2025 coding setting, which METR itself now marks as out of date. It does not measure industry economics or establish causation.
HBS summary of a 2023 experiment showing gains on suitable tasks and shortfalls on others. It measures productivity, not supplier profits, so it neither confirms nor refutes the causal claim.

reviews.rationale: Neither item breaks down industry finances or attributes a substantial share of economic shortfalls to core technical limits. Both are task-level productivity studies pointing in different directions. The packet does not settle the causal claim.
